presentingComplaint: Day-3 post-operative evolving right-sided limb weakness, unsteady gait and painful blurred vision in the left eye following elective total knee replacement.
history: 58-year-old woman with a 14-year history of relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis (EDSS 2.0 at baseline, last relapse 3 years ago, currently off disease-modifying therapy after stopping dimethyl fumarate for elective surgery). Admitted for an elective right total knee replacement. On post-operative day 3 she developed subacute, stuttering onset over 48-72 hours of dragging of the right leg, clumsiness of the right hand, an unsteady wide-based gait and blurring of vision in the left eye with pain on eye movement. She also reports new urinary urgency and frequency. There is no headache, no facial droop and no sudden-onset deficit. Comorbidities: hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus. Polypharmacy: amlodipine, ramipril, metformin, gliclazide, atorvastatin, plus peri-operative enoxaparin, tramadol, ondansetron, omeprazole and regular paracetamol. Bowels normal; no recent fever or dysuria.
examination: Alert, orientated, not toxic. Left relative afferent pupillary defect with reduced visual acuity and impaired colour vision in the left eye; painful eye movements. Right-sided pyramidal weakness (MRC 4/5) with increased tone, brisk reflexes and an extensor right plantar. Sensory examination shows reduced vibration and proprioception in the right lower limb with a subtle T6 sensory level. Cerebellar testing reveals right-sided dysmetria and an ataxic, wide-based gait. No neck stiffness. Surgical wound clean and dry; no calf tenderness or swelling; no catheter in situ.
imaging: MRI brain and whole spine with gadolinium: multiple T2/FLAIR hyperintense lesions in a periventricular, juxtacortical and infratentorial distribution with a new gadolinium-enhancing (open-ring) lesion in the left corona radiata and a short-segment enhancing lesion in the cervical cord; findings meet dissemination in space and time. No acute diffusion restriction to suggest infarction and no cord compression.
microbiology: No microbiological source identified. Urinalysis, urine culture and blood cultures negative; afebrile throughout, excluding an infective pseudo-relapse (Uhthoff phenomenon) as the sole explanation.
differentialDiagnoses: Acute multiple sclerosis relapse (new inflammatory demyelinating activity)
Ischaemic stroke / lacunar syndrome (peri-operative, vascular risk factors)
Pseudo-relapse from occult post-operative infection or metabolic derangement (Uhthoff)
finalDiagnosis: Acute relapse of relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis, confirmed by a new gadolinium-enhancing demyelinating lesion on MRI with concordant clinical worsening (left optic neuritis, right pyramidal-sensory syndrome and cerebellar ataxia), infection and vascular causes excluded.
citations: ABN (Association of British Neurologists) — Management of multiple sclerosis relapse — 2015
ECTRIMS/EAN — Pharmacological treatment of multiple sclerosis — 2018
stewardship: Non-infective, inflammatory presentation: no antibiotics are indicated. The peri-operative context mandates an active infection screen (urinalysis/culture, blood cultures, wound review, temperature charting) BEFORE attributing symptoms to a relapse and before high-dose corticosteroids, because occult sepsis or a UTI can produce an Uhthoff pseudo-relapse and steroids would be harmful if infection were present. Antimicrobials should only be started if a source is confirmed; empirical antibiotics for these neurological symptoms would be inappropriate. Treatment of the confirmed relapse is a short course of high-dose corticosteroid (e.g., IV or oral methylprednisolone 500-1000 mg daily for 3-5 days) with glucose monitoring given diabetes, gastroprotection and VTE prophylaxis; escalate/resume disease-modifying therapy via neurology.
contraindications: Do not give high-dose corticosteroids until active infection is excluded in this post-operative patient
Corticosteroids will destabilise glycaemic control in this diabetic patient - requires capillary glucose monitoring and possible insulin cover
Avoid attributing deficit to relapse without MRI - exclude spinal cord compression and ischaemic stroke first
Polypharmacy: review interactions (tramadol lowers seizure threshold; QT and serotonergic load with ondansetron) before adding drugs
edgeCases: Uhthoff phenomenon: post-operative fever or UTI can transiently reproduce old deficits (pseudo-relapse) - no new enhancing lesion, resolves with cooling/treating the trigger
Older-onset relapse can be mistaken for peri-operative ischaemic stroke; subacute stuttering evolution over days and multifocal CNS signs favour demyelination
New enhancing cord lesion must be distinguished from compressive myelopathy after positioning during surgery
Stopping disease-modifying therapy peri-operatively (especially natalizumab/fingolimod-class) can precipitate rebound disease activity
expectedMaiK: Recognise an acute MS relapse in a known RRMS patient (multifocal subacute CNS deficit), confirm with gadolinium-enhanced MRI, actively exclude a peri-operative infective/metabolic pseudo-relapse and stroke, then treat with high-dose corticosteroids - no antibiotics.
expectedNextQuestions: What is the tempo and evolution of the deficit (subacute over days vs sudden)?
Any fever, dysuria, wound or line infection to suggest an Uhthoff pseudo-relapse?
Prior MS relapse history, current/most recent disease-modifying therapy and when it was stopped?
Any preceding painful monocular visual loss or bladder disturbance?
